exampleAnswers.Purpose and audience: Compare available hours and committed work, with explicit assumptions about capacity.
exampleAnswers.Working context: This fictional three-person team plans one week at a time. Available hours already exclude leave and recurring meetings. Committed hours are estimates for the named work, not a measure of individual performance.
exampleAnswers.Example records:
Person: Maya · Available hours: 30 · Committed hours: 26 · Unallocated hours: 4
Person: Leo · Available hours: 24 · Committed hours: 22 · Unallocated hours: 2
Person: Sam · Available hours: 28 · Committed hours: 20 · Unallocated hours: 8
exampleAnswers.Content decisions:
Read the spare capacity: The team has 14 unallocated hours across 82 available hours. Sam has the largest buffer, but work should move only when the skills and handover cost make sense.
Protect the assumptions: Do not add a full working week on top of the available-hours figure. Leave and meetings have already been removed. Revisit commitments when a task grows or an unexpected support request arrives.
A practical adjustment: Keep Leo’s remaining two hours for review and interruptions. Ask Sam to prepare the workshop checklist if the handover is small. Confirm the change with both people before treating it as the new plan.
exampleAnswers.Format and interaction: capacity layout; section navigation and expandable detail where useful; matching portrait document PDF.
exampleAnswers.Sharing and provenance: A hypothetical example informed by Claw Me’s small-team and Agent workflows. These are not Pete’s actual clients, finances, travel plans, research results, or commitments. Keep the real adaptation private until the owner chooses to share.
